subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 13 periods = 520 minutes
Total: 13 periods · 8h 40min

periods.stage_label: Observe and sort by indicator response
periods.activity_description: Students test a set of household samples — lemon juice, soap solution, baking soda solution, tap water, and sugar solution — with blue and red litmus papers, record the colour changes in a table, and sort each sample into an initial grouping.

roles.role_description: Sets up the testing stations, introduces litmus as a natural dye from lichens, and prompts students to record observations without yet naming the groups.
Test each sample with both litmus papers, record colour changes, and propose a sorting scheme based solely on what they observe.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the chapter's opening science fair scenario and establishes the idea of an indicator as a substance that signals something about another substance through colour change.
Groups carry out litmus paper tests on all samples, recording colour changes systematically in a prepared observation table.
Groups propose their own sorting rules and share them briefly with the class, noting where groupings agree or differ.

Teacher consolidates the three groups — acidic (blue turns red), basic (red turns blue), neutral (no change) — and links the behaviour to litmus being derived from lichens found in clean-air environments.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the chapter's entry point, so orient students to the central question: how can we tell what kind of substance something is without tasting it? Watch for the common error of students concluding that if blue litmus does not change, the substance must be basic — help them see that both papers must be tested before a grouping is made. A useful checkpoint is whether each group has a sample in all three columns before the consolidation.

periods.stage_label: Observe and sort by indicator response
periods.activity_title: Expanding the litmus test — full sample set
periods.activity_description: Students extend the litmus testing to the remaining samples — amla juice, tamarind water, vinegar, lime water, washing powder solution, and salt solution — completing the full Activity 2.1 classification table, then connect the acidic group to taste evidence from Activity 2.2.

roles.role_description: Test all remaining samples with both litmus papers, complete the classification table, and add a taste/texture observation column linking sourness and slipperiness to their sorted groups.

Circulates to check that students are testing both papers for every sample and prompts the taste-and-texture connection to the acidic and basic columns without endorsing tasting unknown substances in the lab.

time_bands.activity: Brief recap of the previous unit's groupings; students identify which samples still need to be tested.
Groups test the remaining samples and fill in the complete observation table, noting colour changes for both litmus papers.

Students add a column connecting the acidic group to sourness (citric acid in lemon, ascorbic acid in amla, tartaric acid in tamarind, acetic acid in vinegar) and the basic group to soapy or bitter character, drawing on Activity 2.2 observations.
Whole-class share-out consolidates the completed three-group classification and introduces the named acids — citric, tartaric, ascorbic, oxalic — as naturally occurring acids in food.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the previous unit's partial table, students now complete the full classification and begin connecting chemical nature to sensory properties. Watch for the misconception that all sour substances are always acidic regardless of concentration — the chapter grounds the acid identification in indicator behaviour, not taste alone. Probing question: 'Can two substances in the same group give different colour intensities on the litmus paper? Does that change their group?'
materials: Completed observation table from previous unit

periods.stage_label: Observe and sort by indicator response
periods.activity_title: Red rose extract — a second indicator
periods.activity_description: Students prepare a red rose petal extract through crushing and filtering, then test the full sample set using the extract, recording the colours observed in acidic and basic solutions, and compare the groupings produced by this indicator with those from litmus testing.

roles.role_description: Prepare the rose petal extract, test each sample, record the colour changes (red in acidic, green in basic), and compare the new groupings with their completed litmus table.
Guides the preparation procedure (crushing and filtering) and directs students to ask whether both indicators always agree on a sample's group.

time_bands.activity: Students prepare the red rose extract by crushing petals in water and filtering the liquid into a clean container, following Activity 2.3 steps.
Groups test several samples from the full set — covering representatives of all three groups — with the rose extract and record observed colours.

Students compare the new groupings with their litmus table, noting that acidic samples show red and basic samples show green with the rose extract, and that all three groups are correctly identified by both indicators.

Teacher introduces the broader family of plant-based indicators — beetroot, purple cabbage, turmeric, jamun, red hibiscus — and the hydrangea observation as an example of a plant whose flower colour indicates soil acidity.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous two units established groupings through litmus; this unit asks students to interrogate whether a different indicator produces consistent groupings. Watch for students who expect the extract colour to be identical to litmus colour changes — clarify that each indicator has its own characteristic colour response, but the grouping it produces should match. The inquiry question to keep live is: 'If a new plant extract gives three distinct colours across our samples, can it serve as an indicator?'
materials: Mortar and pestle or flat stone
Full sample set from previous units
Observation table with litmus data already filled

periods.stage_label: Observe and sort by indicator response
periods.activity_description: Students prepare turmeric paper strips, test samples to discover that turmeric detects only basic substances (yellow turns red), and then investigate onion-soaked strips as an olfactory indicator, recording odour change observations for acidic and basic samples.

roles.role_description: Prepare turmeric strips following Activity 2.5, test samples and record colour changes, then use onion-soaked strips and record odour responses in Activity 2.6.

Introduces the limitation of turmeric paper — it cannot distinguish acidic from neutral — and connects the olfactory indicator concept to the broader class of indicators that respond through senses other than sight.

time_bands.activity: Students prepare turmeric paper strips by soaking filter paper in turmeric paste and allowing them to dry partially, following Activity 2.5.
Groups test samples from all three groups with turmeric paper, record colour changes, and identify the pattern: only basic samples turn the paper red; acidic and neutral samples leave it unchanged.
Students use onion-soaked strips on one acidic and one basic sample, recording whether the characteristic odour of onion is detectable or masked, following Activity 2.6.

Teacher highlights the difference between turmeric paper and litmus paper in their ability to distinguish all three groups, and introduces the Know a Scientist feature on Acharya Prafulla Chandra Ray.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit completes the indicator suite and surfaces a critical distinction: not all indicators can distinguish all three groups. Students frequently assume that a substance that does not change turmeric paper must be neutral — push them to articulate that turmeric paper can only confirm 'basic' or 'not basic', not sort further. The olfactory indicator activity works well as a quick individual investigation before the group debrief.
materials: Cotton or filter paper for onion strips

periods.stage_label: Compare indicators and classify by chemical nature
periods.activity_title: Mapping indicators — what each one reveals
periods.activity_description: Students consolidate all their observation tables into a single comparison chart showing how each of the three indicators — litmus, rose extract, and turmeric paper — responds to representatives of each group, identifying where indicators agree and where one provides information another cannot.

roles.role_description: Construct a personal consolidation chart from their recorded data, filling in the indicator response for each sample across all three indicators, and annotate where turmeric paper is ambiguous.
Leads a structured discussion connecting the chart to the three chemical nature groups, clarifying the concept of acid-base indicator and the scope and limitation of each indicator tested.

time_bands.activity: Students individually draw a consolidation table with samples as rows and indicator responses (litmus blue, litmus red, rose extract, turmeric paper) as columns, pulling from their earlier observation records.
Teacher-led discussion of the completed chart: where all three indicators agree on acidic, where they agree on basic, and where turmeric paper cannot distinguish acidic from neutral.
Class identifies chemical characteristics associated with each group — sour taste and colour-change behaviour for acids, soapy feel and bitter taste for bases — and links these to the classification.
Teacher formally introduces the term 'acid-base indicator' and distinguishes indicators by the range of groups they can detect, setting up the next unit's deeper classification reasoning.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous four units generated raw observational data; this unit is the first moment of structured synthesis across indicators. Watch for students who treat the comparison as just copying tables — prompt them to explain why turmeric paper cannot replace litmus by asking: 'If you had only turmeric paper, which group could you never confirm?' The consolidation chart produced here is a resource for the next unit, so ensure every student completes it before the unit closes.

periods.stage_label: Compare indicators and classify by chemical nature
periods.activity_title: Classification reasoning — which indicator would you choose?
periods.activity_description: Students receive a set of mystery scenario cards describing a situation where only a specific indicator is available and must reason which group a substance can and cannot be confirmed as belonging to, then justify their reasoning in writing.

roles.role_description: Work through scenario cards, identifying for each available indicator what conclusion can be drawn, what cannot be concluded, and why, recording justifications in their workbooks.
Poses the scenario cards as a structured inquiry and monitors group reasoning, probing for justifications rather than answers.

time_bands.activity: Teacher distributes scenario cards and frames the task: for each card, the group must state what the available indicator can and cannot tell you about the substance.
Groups work through the scenario cards, using their consolidation charts from the previous unit as reference, and record reasoned conclusions for each scenario.
Groups share their reasoning on one card each; the class evaluates whether the conclusion is warranted by the indicator's known behaviour.

Teacher summarises the classification framework: a substance's chemical nature is determined by consistent indicator evidence, not by a single test, and different indicators have different diagnostic power.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit pushes students beyond recording observations toward justifying classifications — the cognitive step needed for Stage 2. A common difficulty is that students believe a non-response always means neutral; use the scenario cards to create situations where a non-response to turmeric paper leaves the classification genuinely open. Encourage groups to articulate their reasoning aloud before writing it, which surfaces incomplete logic early.
materials: Scenario cards (teacher-prepared, grounded in chapter samples)
Students' consolidation charts from previous unit

periods.stage_label: Observe and describe the neutralisation reaction
periods.activity_description: Students carry out the lemon juice and lime water experiment from section 2.2, adding lime water dropwise to lemon juice in blue litmus solution, observing the colour shift from red through to blue, and recording the point at which the solution is neither acidic nor basic.

roles.role_description: Add lime water incrementally to acidic lemon juice with litmus indicator, record colour at each addition, and identify the transition point where the colour is intermediate and the solution is neutral.
Demonstrates the first addition for the class and introduces the term 'neutralisation' once students have observed and described the colour transition independently.

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates the setup: lemon juice in a cup with a few drops of blue litmus solution, then adds a small amount of lime water and draws students' attention to the colour change before they begin their own trials.

Groups carry out the experiment, adding lime water dropwise and recording the colour of the solution after each addition until the solution shifts from red toward an intermediate and then blue colour.
Students record the transition point in their tables and describe in one sentence what seems to have happened to the acid when sufficient base was added.
Teacher introduces the term 'neutralisation reaction' to name the phenomenon students observed and asks them to predict what products might have formed.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the opening of the neutralisation strand, and it is important that students encounter the colour-transition evidence before hearing the definition. A common error is students thinking that the base 'destroys' the acid rather than reacting with it to produce new substances — keep the word 'products' central. The prediction of products at the close sets up the next unit's conceptual work.

periods.stage_label: Observe and describe the neutralisation reaction
periods.activity_title: Products of neutralisation — salt, water, and heat
periods.activity_description: Students analyse what was produced in the neutralisation experiment — salt, water, and heat — and connect these products to the general equation Acid + Base → Salt + Water + Heat, recording the equation and its meaning in their own words.

roles.role_description: Explains the three products of neutralisation using the experiment observations as evidence, introduces the chemical equation, and explains what 'salt' means in a chemistry context versus table salt.
Record the general equation, write a sentence explaining what each product is and where it came from, and connect the heat production to the observation that the reaction releases energy.

time_bands.activity: Teacher revisits the previous unit's prediction of products and systematically identifies salt, water, and heat as the three products of a neutralisation reaction, with reference to the lemon juice–lime water experiment.

Students record the general equation in their workbooks and write a plain-language explanation of what happens: the acid and base react and are consumed, producing a new substance (salt), water, and releasing heat.
Teacher clarifies that 'salt' in chemistry refers to a class of compounds, not only sodium chloride (table salt), and gives the example of the product formed in the lemon juice–lime water reaction.
Quick paired check: students explain the equation to a partner and the partner must identify which product accounts for the temperature change felt when the reaction occurs.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is the conceptual anchor for the neutralisation strand; the previous unit provided the observation, and this unit provides the explanation. The most persistent misconception here is that 'salt' means cooking salt — make the chemistry definition explicit and distinct. If students struggled to observe heat in the previous unit, note that the heat effect may be subtle at small volumes and that the equation represents the general principle.
materials: Chalkboard or display surface for equation

periods.stage_label: Observe and describe the neutralisation reaction
periods.activity_description: Students revisit the chapter's opening science fair mystery — the message revealed on turmeric-coated paper — and use their knowledge of turmeric as an indicator and the behaviour of soap as a basic substance to explain the mechanism step by step.

roles.role_description: Reconstruct the mechanism of the mystery: turmeric paper coated the base paper, soap solution (basic) was used as ink, and the basic soap turned the turmeric paper red where it was applied, revealing the message.
Guides the reconstruction with targeted questions — what was the paper coated with, what property of soap made it act as 'ink', and what indicator principle explains the colour change.

time_bands.activity: Teacher re-presents the opening science fair scenario and asks groups to try to explain the mystery using what they now know about indicators and neutralisation.
Groups discuss and reconstruct the mechanism, identifying turmeric's behaviour with basic substances (yellow to red) and the role of soap as the basic writing medium.
Groups share their explanations and the class evaluates them for completeness — does the explanation name the indicator, the substance tested, and the colour change observed?

Teacher confirms the chapter's own explanation and connects this application back to all three indicators studied, noting that the mystery uses exactly the kind of indicator knowledge built across this chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous two units built the neutralisation concept; this unit uses the mystery as a low-stakes application to consolidate indicator knowledge before moving to daily-life neutralisation contexts. Watch for students who guess the mechanism without invoking the indicator principle — require them to name the specific colour change and identify which indicator is involved. This unit also provides a natural bridge to the next stage, where neutralisation is applied to real-world problems.
materials: Chapter narrative text describing the science fair mystery

periods.stage_label: Explain neutralisation as a chemical change with real-world applications
periods.activity_title: Neutralisation in the body — the ant bite case
periods.activity_description: Students analyse the ant bite scenario from section 2.3 — formic acid injected into skin, baking soda applied as remedy — identifying the acid, the base, the products, and explaining why the reaction relieves the pain.

roles.role_description: Presents the ant bite scenario, identifies formic acid as the injected substance, and connects the remedy to the neutralisation equation, asking students to map the scenario onto the general equation.
Map the ant bite scenario onto the general neutralisation equation, labelling the acid (formic acid), the base (baking soda), and the products, and write a causal explanation of pain relief.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the ant bite scenario and asks students to identify from their prior knowledge what kind of substance is injected and what kind of substance is applied as a remedy.

Students individually map the scenario onto the general equation — Acid (formic acid) + Base (baking soda) → Salt + Water + Heat — and write two sentences explaining why neutralisation relieves the pain.
Pairs compare their explanations, checking that both identify the acid, the base, and the connection between removing the acid and reducing the irritation.
Teacher consolidates the causal chain and introduces the idea that this is an example of neutralisation as a chemical change, where both reactants are consumed and new substances are formed.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the first of three daily-life applications and begins the transition from describing neutralisation to explaining it as a chemical change with a cause-effect chain. A common difficulty is that students say the baking soda 'removes' the acid rather than reacting with it — insist on the language of chemical change and products. The paired comparison before consolidation helps surface incomplete causal chains.

periods.stage_label: Explain neutralisation as a chemical change with real-world applications
periods.activity_title: Soil correction — choosing the right remedy
periods.activity_description: Students analyse the soil correction scenario from section 2.3, distinguishing between soil that is too acidic (corrected by adding lime) and soil that is too basic (corrected by adding compost), and explain why different remedies are used in each case.

roles.role_description: Analyse both soil scenarios, identify the chemical nature of the problem and the remedy in each, and write a causal explanation of why each remedy works in terms of neutralisation.
Poses the two scenarios as a comparative inquiry and asks groups to articulate what determines which remedy is chosen, guiding them toward the neutralisation principle.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents both soil scenarios side by side — too acidic (lime added) and too basic (compost added) — and asks groups to identify what each remedy does chemically.

Groups discuss and write explanations for both scenarios, mapping each onto the neutralisation equation and explaining the role of the compost as a source of organic acids that neutralise the basic soil.
Groups share explanations and the class evaluates whether the explanation correctly names the direction of neutralisation in each scenario.
Teacher highlights that this is neutralisation used as a tool for control: understanding the chemical nature of a problem directs the choice of remedy.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the previous unit's ant bite case, this unit requires students to apply neutralisation in both directions — correcting acidity and correcting basicity — which tests genuine understanding of the reaction rather than a memorised single example. Watch for the misconception that lime always corrects any soil problem; the chapter is explicit that too-basic soil requires organic acids, not lime. The comparative structure of this unit is the key pedagogical move.
materials: Soil scenario description cards (teacher-prepared from chapter text)

periods.stage_label: Explain neutralisation as a chemical change with real-world applications
periods.activity_title: Industrial waste — designing a neutralisation solution
periods.activity_description: Students analyse the factory waste scenario from section 2.3 — acidic waste released into a lake harming fish — and reason about what must be done to the waste before release, then test a model version by adding a basic substance to a vinegar solution monitored with litmus.

roles.role_description: First reason through the factory waste scenario in writing, identifying the problem substance and the type of remedy needed, then carry out a hands-on model test: add baking soda solution dropwise to vinegar with litmus indicator and record the neutralisation point.
Connects the scenario reasoning to the hands-on test and asks students to identify when the waste is safe to release by using the litmus indicator as a monitoring tool.

time_bands.activity: Students read the factory waste scenario and write a brief explanation identifying the acidic waste as the problem and describing why it harms fish, connecting to the idea that aquatic life is harmed by extreme acidity.
Groups carry out the model test — adding baking soda solution dropwise to vinegar with litmus indicator — and record colour at each addition, identifying the point where the solution is neutral.
Students connect the model test to the scenario: the indicator tells the factory when neutralisation is complete and the waste is safe to release.
Teacher draws together all three daily-life applications and frames the closing question for the next unit: what makes an application of neutralisation an example of a chemical change?

periods.teacher_notes: This unit combines the analytical work from the previous two units with a hands-on model, making the real-world scenario concrete. Students sometimes overlook the role of the indicator as a monitoring tool rather than just a classification tool — connect back to Stage 1 explicitly and ask: 'How is the indicator being used differently here than when we first sorted samples?' The closing question sets up the final unit's integrative reasoning.

periods.stage_label: Explain neutralisation as a chemical change with real-world applications
periods.activity_title: Bringing both strands together — classify, then apply
periods.activity_description: Students receive an unseen scenario involving a new acidic or basic substance and must classify it using indicator logic, then select and justify a neutralisation remedy, demonstrating integrated use of both classification and chemical-change reasoning in a single written response.

roles.role_description: Read the unseen scenario, apply indicator classification reasoning to identify the nature of the substance, select an appropriate neutralisation remedy, and write a connected causal explanation linking classification to remedy choice to products.
Presents the scenario, clarifies that this is an individual task drawing on both strands of the chapter, and uses responses to identify the range of reasoning quality across the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents an unseen scenario — for example, a lake that turns blue litmus red and harms aquatic life — and clarifies the two-part task: classify the substance and design a remedy.
Students individually write their response, using their knowledge of indicators to classify and their knowledge of neutralisation to justify the remedy and name the products.

Teacher selects two or three responses with contrasting levels of causal detail and reads them aloud (anonymised), asking the class to identify which response most fully connects classification to remedy to products.

Teacher closes by naming the two strands of the chapter — classifying substances by their chemical nature, and understanding neutralisation as a chemical change — and affirms that students have worked with both.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the chapter's closing unit and the first moment students are asked to integrate both strands in a single unseen task. Watch for responses that classify correctly but then apply a remedy without connecting it to neutralisation products — the strongest responses will name the acid, the base, and at least one product. The anonymous read-aloud of contrasting responses is a powerful formative move that helps students self-calibrate without comparison to named peers.
materials: Unseen scenario card (teacher-prepared from chapter content)

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Observe and sort by indicator response
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students test household samples with litmus papers, red rose extract, turmeric paper, and onion olfactory strips, recording colour changes and sorting samples into acidic, basic, and neutral groups across all three indicator types.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can test a substance with at least two different natural indicators, record the colour changes observed, and correctly sort the substance into the acidic, basic, or neutral group based on consistent indicator evidence.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Compare indicators and classify by chemical nature
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students consolidate observation data into a cross-indicator comparison chart and reason through scenario cards to evaluate which indicator can and cannot confirm a given classification, justifying their conclusions in writing.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can compare the diagnostic scope of litmus paper, red rose extract, and turmeric paper, and justify why two or more indicators may be needed to confirm a substance's chemical nature.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Observe and describe the neutralisation reaction
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students carry out the lemon juice–lime water neutralisation experiment, identify the products (salt, water, heat) and the general equation, and apply the mechanism to explain the science fair mystery.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe the neutralisation reaction — including its reactants, products, and the role of an indicator in tracking it — and apply this description to explain an unfamiliar example of a base acting on an acid-sensitive indicator.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Explain neutralisation as a chemical change with real-world applications
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students analyse three daily-life neutralisation scenarios (ant bite, soil correction, industrial waste), map each onto the general equation, and in the closing unit integrate classification and chemical-change reasoning to respond to an unseen scenario.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify an unfamiliar substance as acidic or basic using indicator logic and explain how applying an appropriate acid or base as a remedy constitutes a neutralisation reaction — a chemical change — naming the products and their significance.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and sort by indicator response
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can test a substance with at least two different natural indicators, record the colour changes observed, and correctly sort the substance into the acidic, basic, or neutral group based on consistent indicator evidence.

competency.competency_text: Classification of matter by chemical characteristics — identifying substances as acidic, basic, or neutral using natural indicators.

assessment_items.question_text: A student tests a sample with blue litmus paper and observes no colour change. The student concludes the sample is neutral. Which of the following best describes this conclusion?

options.label: A
options.text: The conclusion is correct because blue litmus paper alone can confirm all three groups.

options.label: B
options.text: The conclusion is correct because only basic substances change the colour of blue litmus paper.

options.label: C
options.text: The conclusion may be wrong because red litmus paper must also be tested before the group can be confirmed.

options.label: D
options.text: The conclusion may be wrong because the student should have used turmeric paper instead of litmus paper.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Indicates the student believes a single litmus paper is sufficient to confirm all three groups, conflating absence of change on blue litmus with neutral classification.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates the student has the directionality of litmus correct for basic substances but has not recognised that a non-change on blue litmus could also be produced by an acidic substance.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Indicates the student has learned about the limitations of turmeric paper but has misapplied that knowledge by suggesting it as the primary substitute rather than completing the two-paper litmus test.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the written stem can be prompted by the teacher to re-enact the test physically: 'What would happen if this sample were acidic — what would blue litmus show?' This re-enactment pathway leads to the same reasoning without requiring abstract recall.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and sort by indicator response
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can test a substance with at least two different natural indicators, record the colour changes observed, and correctly sort the substance into the acidic, basic, or neutral group based on consistent indicator evidence.

competency.competency_text: Classification of matter by chemical characteristics — identifying substances as acidic, basic, or neutral using natural indicators.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Sample | Blue litmus | Red litmus | Turmeric paper
P | No change | No change | No change
Q | Turns red | No change | No change
R | No change | Turns blue | Turns red
S | No change | No change | No change
assessment_items.question_text: A student records indicator results for four samples. Refer to the table provided. Which two samples belong to the same chemical nature group?

options.label: A
options.text: P and R, because both left turmeric paper unchanged.

options.label: B
options.text: P and S, because neither caused a colour change in any of the three indicators.

options.label: C
options.text: Q and R, because both caused a colour change in at least one indicator.

options.label: D
options.text: Q and S, because both left red litmus paper unchanged.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Indicates the student is using 'caused a change' as a grouping criterion without distinguishing the direction of change, conflating the acidic group (Q) with the basic group (R).
what_each_option_reveals.A: Indicates the student is over-relying on turmeric paper as a definitive sorter — they know turmeric detects only basic substances but have drawn a neutral grouping from a non-change, ignoring the litmus evidence that distinguishes P (neutral) from R (basic).
what_each_option_reveals.D: Indicates the student is using a single column (red litmus unchanged) as a grouping criterion, not recognising that both Q (acidic — blue litmus turns red) and S (neutral) share that single non-response.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle to read the table systematically can be asked to process one column at a time, marking each cell before comparing rows. This step-by-step column-reading strategy leads to the same classification outcome through a supported pathway.

assessment_items.stage_label: Compare indicators and classify by chemical nature
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can compare the diagnostic scope of litmus paper, red rose extract, and turmeric paper, and justify why two or more indicators may be needed to confirm a substance's chemical nature.

competency.competency_text: Classification of matter by chemical characteristics — identifying substances as acidic, basic, or neutral using natural indicators.

assessment_items.question_text: A student has only turmeric paper available. After testing a substance, the turmeric paper shows no colour change. What can the student correctly conclude?

options.label: A
options.text: The substance is acidic, because basic substances always turn turmeric paper red.

options.label: B
options.text: The substance is basic, because turmeric paper only changes colour when a non-basic substance is tested.

options.label: C
options.text: The substance is either acidic or neutral, and a second indicator is needed to distinguish between these two groups.

options.label: D
options.text: The substance is neutral, because it caused no change in the indicator.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Indicates the student has not internalised the limitation of turmeric paper — they are treating a non-change as a positive confirmation of neutral status, which requires evidence from a more discriminating indicator.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Indicates partial knowledge: the student knows that basic substances turn turmeric paper red but has incorrectly reasoned that a non-change must mean acidic, ignoring the neutral possibility.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates a reversal of the indicator's known behaviour — the student may have confused the direction of the turmeric paper response, believing it changes with non-basic substances.

MCQ.inclusivity: For students who find the abstract reasoning difficult, the teacher can present two physical strips — one dipped in lime water (red), one dipped in lemon juice (unchanged) — and ask: 'Can you tell from the unchanged strip alone whether the substance was acidic or neutral?' This physical referent makes the limitation concrete.

assessment_items.stage_label: Compare indicators and classify by chemical nature
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can compare the diagnostic scope of litmus paper, red rose extract, and turmeric paper, and justify why two or more indicators may be needed to confirm a substance's chemical nature.

competency.competency_text: Classification of matter by chemical characteristics — identifying substances as acidic, basic, or neutral using natural indicators.

assessment_items.question_text: Red rose extract turns red in an acidic solution and green in a basic solution. Litmus paper turns red in acidic solutions and blue in basic solutions. A student claims that red rose extract can replace litmus paper entirely in all classification tasks. Which of the following is the strongest reason to disagree with this claim?

options.label: A
options.text: Both indicators can identify all three chemical nature groups, so neither has a scope advantage over the other for classification.

options.label: B
options.text: Red rose extract cannot be used because it is not a standardised laboratory chemical like litmus.

options.label: C
options.text: Red rose extract cannot distinguish acidic from neutral because both give a red colour, unlike litmus which gives different colours for each group.

options.label: D
options.text: Red rose extract gives a green colour in basic solutions, but litmus paper gives a blue colour, so the indicators are completely different and cannot be compared.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Indicates the student is focused on the surface feature (different colours) rather than diagnostic scope, and has not evaluated whether both indicators can classify all three groups.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates the student is applying an external criterion (standardisation) not grounded in the chapter's content about natural indicators — a recall of an out-of-context notion about laboratory chemicals.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Indicates the student has confused the known limitation of turmeric paper (cannot distinguish acidic from neutral) with red rose extract, which according to the chapter gives distinct colours for acidic (red) and basic (green) solutions, with neutral giving a third distinct colour.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain can be directed to their consolidation chart from the comparison units and asked to check: 'What colour does red rose extract give for each group?' Reading the chart re-activates the classification evidence without requiring pure recall.

assessment_items.stage_label: Compare indicators and classify by chemical nature
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can compare the diagnostic scope of litmus paper, red rose extract, and turmeric paper, and justify why two or more indicators may be needed to confirm a substance's chemical nature.

competency.competency_text: Classification of matter by chemical characteristics — identifying substances as acidic, basic, or neutral using natural indicators.

assessment_items.question_text: A student uses only turmeric paper to test three substances — lemon juice, baking soda solution, and salt solution. All three show no colour change. The student concludes that all three substances belong to the same group. Explain why this conclusion is incorrect and describe what the student should do to correctly classify all three substances.
expected_elements: Identification that turmeric paper turns red only in the presence of basic substances and shows no change for both acidic and neutral substances.
Explanation that lemon juice is acidic and salt solution is neutral, so they cannot belong to the same group even though both leave turmeric paper unchanged.
A description of using litmus paper (both blue and red) or red rose extract as a second indicator that can distinguish acidic from neutral substances, thereby completing the classification.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to write an explanation can be offered a sentence-starter approach: 'Turmeric paper only tells us if a substance is _____. It cannot tell apart _____ and _____ because both _____.This means the student should also use _____ to finish classifying the substances.' This scaffold leads to the same three-element response through guided sentence completion.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and describe the neutralisation reaction
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe the neutralisation reaction — including its reactants, products, and the role of an indicator in tracking it — and apply this description to explain an unfamiliar example of a base acting on an acid-sensitive indicator.

competency.competency_text: Changes in matter — understanding neutralisation as a chemical change producing salt, water, and heat.

assessment_items.question_text: In the lemon juice and lime water experiment, a student adds lime water dropwise to lemon juice that contains blue litmus solution. The solution first turns red, then shows an intermediate colour, and finally turns blue. What does the blue colour at the end indicate?

options.label: A
options.text: The acid in the lemon juice has been fully neutralised and the solution has become basic due to excess lime water.

options.label: B
options.text: The lemon juice has been diluted so much that it is no longer detectable by litmus.

options.label: C
options.text: The lime water has changed colour because it was exposed to air during the experiment.

options.label: D
options.text: The litmus solution has run out of acid to detect, so it returns to its original blue colour regardless of the solution's nature.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates the student is interpreting the colour change as a dilution effect rather than a chemical reaction, not distinguishing between physical mixing and a neutralisation reaction.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Indicates the student is confusing the lime water colour change with a physical property change due to air exposure, rather than recognising the litmus response as a chemical indicator of the solution's nature.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Indicates the student believes litmus has a fixed number of 'uses' or responses and reverts after detecting acid, a misconception about how indicators work as responsive chemical substances.

MCQ.inclusivity: For students who are uncertain, the teacher can replay the sequence verbally — 'What does red litmus colour mean? What does blue mean? What did the solution contain at the start?' — to rebuild the indicator logic before the student selects an option.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and describe the neutralisation reaction
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe the neutralisation reaction — including its reactants, products, and the role of an indicator in tracking it — and apply this description to explain an unfamiliar example of a base acting on an acid-sensitive indicator.

competency.competency_text: Changes in matter — understanding neutralisation as a chemical change producing salt, water, and heat.

assessment_items.question_text: In the science fair mystery, a message was written on paper coated with turmeric solution using soap solution as the writing medium. The message appeared as red markings on a yellow background. Which of the following correctly explains why the message appeared?

options.label: A
options.text: Soap solution is acidic, and acidic substances turn turmeric paper from yellow to red where they are applied.

options.label: B
options.text: Soap solution is basic, and basic substances turn turmeric paper from yellow to red where they are applied.

options.label: C
options.text: Soap solution is neutral and reacts with the turmeric coating to produce a red pigment through a neutralisation reaction.

options.label: D
options.text: The turmeric coating reacts with the paper fibres when wet, and any liquid applied would produce a red colour.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Indicates the student has confused the direction of the turmeric paper response — they know turmeric paper changes colour but have incorrectly assigned the colour change to acidic rather than basic substances.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Indicates the student is conflating neutralisation with the indicator response: they have introduced neutralisation as an explanation for a colour change that is simply the indicator responding to a basic substance.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Indicates the student has abandoned the chemical indicator framework entirely and is proposing a physical mechanism — wetness causing colour change — that is not grounded in the chapter's explanation of turmeric paper behaviour.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who cannot recall whether soap is acidic or basic can be directed to their classification table from the earlier units, where soap solution was sorted into the basic group using litmus evidence, before applying that group assignment to the turmeric paper response.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and describe the neutralisation reaction
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe the neutralisation reaction — including its reactants, products, and the role of an indicator in tracking it — and apply this description to explain an unfamiliar example of a base acting on an acid-sensitive indicator.

competency.competency_text: Changes in matter — understanding neutralisation as a chemical change producing salt, water, and heat.

assessment_items.question_text: A student mixes an acidic solution and a basic solution in the correct amounts. Write the general equation for this reaction and name the three products. Then state two pieces of evidence the student could observe during the experiment to confirm that the reaction has occurred.
expected_elements: The general equation: Acid + Base → Salt + Water + Heat.
Correct naming of all three products: a salt, water, and heat.
One observable piece of evidence: a colour change in an indicator (e.g., litmus changing from red to an intermediate colour or blue) showing the acidic nature has been neutralised.
A second observable piece of evidence: warmth or a rise in temperature of the solution, indicating heat has been released.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who remember the equation but struggle to describe evidence can be prompted: 'In the lemon juice experiment, what did you see change as you added lime water, and what did you feel if you touched the container?' These two experiential prompts connect the abstract equation to the concrete observations from the activity.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain neutralisation as a chemical change with real-world applications
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify an unfamiliar substance as acidic or basic using indicator logic and explain how applying an appropriate acid or base as a remedy constitutes a neutralisation reaction — a chemical change — naming the products and their significance.

competency.competency_text: Changes in matter — understanding neutralisation as a chemical change producing salt, water, and heat.

assessment_items.question_text: A factory releases waste water into a river. Tests show the waste water turns blue litmus red. The factory treats the waste water by adding a substance before releasing it. Which substance should the factory add, and why is this an example of a chemical change rather than a physical change?

options.label: A
options.text: Add a basic substance such as lime; this is a chemical change because the acid and base react to form new products — salt, water, and heat — that were not present before.

options.label: B
options.text: Add a basic substance such as lime; this is a physical change because the acid is absorbed by the base rather than reacting with it.

options.label: C
options.text: Add an acidic substance such as vinegar; this strengthens the acidic nature of the waste and makes it easier for the river to break it down naturally.

options.label: D
options.text: Add more water to dilute the acid; this is a physical change because no new substance is formed, only the concentration changes.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Indicates the student is applying a physical intervention (dilution) and does not distinguish between reducing concentration and chemically neutralising the acidic nature — a fundamental confusion between physical and chemical change.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates the student has correctly identified the remedy (basic substance) but holds a misconception about the mechanism — 'absorption' rather than a chemical reaction — suggesting they have not internalised the formation of new products as the defining feature of a chemical change.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Indicates the student has inverted the remedy logic: they may have confused the industrial waste scenario with the soil-correction case where an acid is added to basic soil, or may not have connected the litmus evidence (acid waste) to the correct neutralisation direction.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who choose the correct remedy but struggle to articulate why it is a chemical change can be asked: 'After the lime is added and the reaction is complete, is the acid still there in the water? What is there instead?' This question targets the formation of new substances, which is the defining criterion of a chemical change.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify an unfamiliar substance as acidic or basic using indicator logic and explain how applying an appropriate acid or base as a remedy constitutes a neutralisation reaction — a chemical change — naming the products and their significance.

assessment_items.question_text: A farmer notices that crops are not growing well. Testing the soil, the farmer finds that red litmus paper turns blue in the soil extract. Which of the following correctly identifies the soil problem and the appropriate remedy?

options.label: A
options.text: The soil is too acidic; the farmer should add compost to introduce acids that strengthen the soil's acidic nature.

options.label: B
options.text: The soil is too acidic; the farmer should add lime to neutralise the excess acid.

options.label: C
options.text: The soil is too basic; the farmer should add lime to neutralise the excess base.

options.label: D
options.text: The soil is too basic; the farmer should add organic matter like compost to introduce acids that neutralise the excess base.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates the student has misread the litmus evidence — red litmus turning blue indicates a basic substance, not an acidic one — and has then applied the correct remedy for acidity to an incorrectly identified problem.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Indicates a double error: the student has misread the litmus evidence (same as option A) and has also confused the role of compost, adding it to an already acidic soil rather than to a basic soil.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Indicates the student has correctly read the litmus evidence (basic soil) but has confused the remedies — lime is a base and would worsen a basic soil condition, not correct it.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain about the litmus evidence can be asked to work through the indicator logic first as a separate step: 'What does red litmus turning blue always mean? Write that down before choosing a remedy.' Separating the classification step from the remedy selection makes the two-part reasoning explicit.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify an unfamiliar substance as acidic or basic using indicator logic and explain how applying an appropriate acid or base as a remedy constitutes a neutralisation reaction — a chemical change — naming the products and their significance.

competency.competency_text: Changes in matter — understanding neutralisation as a chemical change producing salt, water, and heat.

assessment_items.question_text: A red ant bite causes pain by injecting a substance into the skin. A person applies baking soda paste to the bite and the pain reduces. Using your knowledge of acids, bases, and neutralisation, explain: (a) why the bite causes pain, (b) why baking soda relieves the pain, and (c) why this is a chemical change rather than simply a physical treatment.
look_for: Identification of formic acid as the pain-causing substance injected by the ant, classifying it as an acidic substance.
Explanation that baking soda is a base and reacts with the formic acid through neutralisation, consuming the acid and producing salt, water, and heat.
A clear causal link between the neutralisation reaction consuming the acid and the reduction of the chemical irritation causing the pain.

Distinction between chemical change (new substances — salt and water — are formed, the acid no longer exists as acid) and physical treatment (which would involve no change to the chemical nature of the injected substance).

ECR.inclusivity: Students who can explain parts (a) and (b) but struggle with part (c) can be supported by the teacher asking: 'After the baking soda has been on the bite for a while, is the formic acid still there in its original form? If new substances have formed, what kind of change is that?' This question sequence targets the chemical change criterion without reducing the cognitive demand.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Scenario | Indicator result | Nature of problem substance | Corrective substance | Nature of corrective | Products of reaction | Why fish / crops / skin are affected
River water from a factory (turns blue litmus red) | | | | | |
Farm soil extract (turns red litmus blue) | | | | | |
Red ant bite on skin (turns blue litmus red) | | | | | |
assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. Three real-world situations each involve a substance that has become too acidic or too basic. For each situation: (1) state the nature of the problem substance based on the indicator result, (2) identify an appropriate corrective substance and state its nature, (3) name the products of the neutralisation reaction, and (4) explain why the organism — fish, crop, or skin — is harmed by the problem and helped by the correction.
assessment_items.scaffold: Use the indicator result column to determine whether the problem substance is acidic or basic. Then decide whether the corrective substance must be a base or an acid. Name one suitable corrective substance from the chapter for each situation. For the products column, write what is always produced when an acid and a base react. For the final column, connect the chemical nature of the problem to the biological harm, and the neutralisation products to the relief.
format_of_output: Completed table with all six columns filled for all three scenarios.
One additional sentence per scenario explaining the causal link between the chemical problem and the biological or environmental harm.

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Classification or sorting task with justification
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The final stage's co-central implied LO requires students to simultaneously apply classification reasoning (identify chemical nature using indicator evidence) and chemical-change reasoning (explain neutralisation as the corrective mechanism); a structured table with a justification column is the most natural vehicle for demonstrating both operations in a single integrated response.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response evidences that the student can read indicator data to classify an unfamiliar substance's chemical nature, select the correct neutralisation remedy, name the products of the chemical change, and construct a causal explanation connecting the chemistry to the real-world biological or environmental consequence — integrating both central competencies of the chapter.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold guides students through the table column by column, preventing the most common failure mode — selecting a remedy without identifying the problem substance's nature first. The final column is where the integration of both strands becomes visible: a student who only knows neutralisation products without connecting them to the biological harm will leave the last column thin. Teachers should read that column as the primary differentiator.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses: correctly classify all three problem substances using the indicator result; name a plausible corrective substance for each; state all three products (salt, water, heat); and write a causal sentence that explicitly connects the removal of the acid or base through neutralisation to the relief of harm. Weak responses: classify one or two scenarios correctly but leave others incomplete; name products without connecting them to harm relief; or describe the corrective action as 'removing' the acid or base rather than reacting with it to form new products.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle to complete all three scenarios independently can be asked to complete only the river water scenario fully, including the final causal sentence, and then compare their reasoning to a partially completed example the teacher provides for the farm soil scenario. This tiered approach maintains the integration demand while reducing the volume for students who need more support.
